row.description: Burnt Fen is an area of low-lying land crossed by the A1101 road between Littleport in Cambridgeshire and Mildenhall in Suffolk [1]. It is surrounded on three sides by rivers, and consists of prime agricultural land [1]. Burnt Fen is located near the eastern borders of the Isle of Ely, Cambridgeshire, although parts of it are also located in Suffolk and Norfolk [1]. The area shows a remarkable amount of archaeological findings of the Mesolithic period [1].
row.card: Mesolithic finds show up in a remarkable amount across this low-lying land. Rivers hem the ground in on three sides, and a road now runs through the prime farmland.

row.description: Soyuqbulaq is a village in Agstafa Rayon, Azerbaijan, where a French-Azerbaijani team discovered nine kurgans dating to the beginning of the 4th millennium BC, making it the oldest kurgan cemetery in Transcaucasia [1]. The site is associated with the Leilatepe archaeological culture, believed to have originated from Near Eastern Ubaid culture migrations to the South Caucasus [1]. The kurgans share a northwest-to-southeast grave alignment with Maikop Culture burials to the north [1]. Notably, the earliest evidence of silver use in the Caucasus was attested at Soyuqbulaq [1].
row.card: The earliest evidence of silver use in the Caucasus comes from this village. A team also found nine burial mounds here, the oldest mound cemetery in Transcaucasia.

row.description: The necropolis of Pranu Muttedu is one of the most important funerary areas of pre-Nuragic Sardinia and is located near Goni [1]. The complex features a high concentration of menhirs—around sixty—second only to the vast site of Biru 'e Concas in Sorgono, where roughly 200 menhirs have been recorded [1]. These are arranged in pairs, alignments, or groups [1]. Other monuments include funerary chambers of various types, originally covered by a tumulus and enclosed within megalithic circles built with stone blocks arranged in concentric rings [1]. The area also contains several domus de janas [1].
row.card: Stone blocks set in rings within rings once enclosed these burial chambers. Mounds once covered them, and around sixty standing stones rise in pairs, lines and groups.

row.description: Vitcos was a residence of Inca nobles and a ceremonial center of the Neo-Inca State (1537–1572) [1]. The archaeological site of ancient Vitcos, called Rosaspata, is in the Vilcabamba District of La Convención Province, Cusco Region in Peru [1]. The ruins are on a ridge overlooking the confluence of two small rivers and the village of Pucyura [1]. The Incas had occupied Vilcabamba, the region in which Vitcos is located, about AD 1450, establishing major centers at Machu Picchu, Choquequirao, Vitcos, and Vilcabamba [1]. Vitcos was often the residence of the rulers of the Neo-Inca state until the Spanish conquest of this last stronghold of the Incas in 1572 [1]. The location of Vitcos was later forgotten until 1911 when explorer Hiram Bingham identified the ruins known to local Peruvians as Rosaspata as ancient Vitcos [1].
row.card: In 1911, explorer Hiram Bingham identified a forgotten place in the ruins on a ridge. Inca nobles once lived in the complex, a ceremonial center above the spot where two small rivers meet.

row.description: The Ringlemere barrow is an archaeological site near Sandwich in the English county of Kent most famous as being the find site of the Ringlemere gold cup [1]. No contemporary burials have been found at the site although later Iron Age ones have since been found along with a Saxon cemetery [1]. Excavation work has continued at the site, funded by English Heritage, the BBC, the British Museum and the Kent Archaeological Society [1]. This work has indicated that the now ploughed-away barrow was as high as 5m and had a diameter of more than 40m [1]. The flat-bottomed ditch that surrounded it was 5–6 m wide and 1.35 m deep [1]. Considerable evidence of much earlier Neolithic activity has now been found on the site including by far the largest assemblage of grooved ware in the county [1].
row.card: A gold cup made this mound famous, though it is now ploughed away. Digs also found much earlier Neolithic activity, with by far the largest assemblage of grooved ware in the county.

row.description: Stantonbury Camp is the site of an Iron Age hill fort near Stanton Prior within the parish of Marksbury in Somerset, England [1]. It is a Scheduled Ancient Monument [1]. The hillfort, which is at the top of an isolated outcrop of Oolitic Limestone, close to the A39 road is on the route of the Wansdyke [1]. Several iron agricultural implements from the site, including blades of sickles or pruning hooks and the iron tip from an ard, now reside in the collection of the British Museum [1].
row.card: Iron blades of sickles or pruning hooks came from this hill fort. The British Museum now holds them, and the Iron Age fort tops an isolated limestone outcrop on the route of the Wansdyke.

row.description: Stabiae was an ancient city situated near the modern town of Castellammare di Stabia and approximately 4.5 km southwest of Pompeii [1]. Like Pompeii, and being only 16 km from Mount Vesuvius, it was largely buried by tephra ash in the 79 AD eruption of Mount Vesuvius, in this case at a shallower depth of up to 5 m [1]. Stabiae is most famous for the Roman villas found near the ancient city which are regarded as some of the most stunning architectural and artistic remains from any Roman villas [1]. The villas were sited on a 50 m high headland overlooking the Gulf of Naples [1]. The settlement at Stabiae arose from as early as the 7th century BC due to the favourable climate and its strategic and commercial significance as evocatively documented by materials found in the vast necropolis discovered in 1957 on via Madonna delle Grazie [1]. Stabiae had a small port which by the 6th century BC had already been overshadowed by the much larger port at Pompeii [1]. The archaeological remains at Stabiae were originally discovered in 1749 by Cavaliere Roque Joaquín de Alcubierre [1].
row.card: Like Pompeii, in 79 AD ash from Mount Vesuvius largely buried this ancient city. The city is most famous for the Roman villas found nearby, on a 50 m high headland over the Gulf of Naples.

row.description: Hattusa, near modern Bogazkale in north-central Turkey, was the capital of the Hittite Empire in the 2nd millennium BC and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986 [1] [2]. The site contains a large temple district, the Buyukkale acropolis, and the nearby rock sanctuary of Yazilikaya with its remarkable relief carvings of gods and goddesses [1] [2]. Excavations since 1906 have yielded thousands of cuneiform tablets in Hittite and Akkadian that documented the empire's administration and diplomacy [1].
row.card: A rock shrine with remarkable carvings of gods stands near this Hittite capital. The site holds a large temple district, and digs since 1906 have yielded thousands of tablets.

row.description: The archaeological site of Sanisera is located in the natural port of Sanitja, next to the Cavalleria Cape or Cap de Cavallería [1]. The first written source that makes reference to the city of Sanisera is the mention which Pliny the Elder makes in his book " Naturalis Historia" in the 1st century AD [1]. A series of amphorae dating from the 1st to the 4th centuries AD started to be found and recovered from the seabed [1]. Excavations carried out between 2008 and 2010 have revealed an ecclesiastical complex at the west side of the port of Sanitja [1]. This complex, which possibly dates from the 6th century AD, consists of a basilica and a large multi-functional building, called Building 10 [1]. Between 2008 and 2011 a necropolis was excavated in the surroundings of the Port of Sanitja [1]. It consists of 44 tombs that form several rows with passageways between rows and tombs [1].
row.card: Pliny the Elder wrote the first mention of this city by a natural port. Its seabed gave up storage jars from the 1st to the 4th centuries AD, and rows of tombs lie beside the port.

row.description: The Temple of Aphrodite at ancient Cassope (Kassope) in Epirus, Greece, is a peripteral hexastyle temple measuring 17.20 x 10.15 metres, located outside the city walls [1] [2]. Aphrodite was the patron goddess of Cassope [1] [2]. Cassope itself is one of the best-preserved examples of a Hippodamian grid-plan city in Greece, with visible remains including cyclopean walls, an agora, a theatre, and private houses [2] [3].
row.card: The city's patron goddess got a temple outside the city walls. Within the walls lies one of the best preserved grid-plan cities in the country, with an agora, a theatre and private houses.

row.description: King Arthur's Round Table is a Neolithic henge in the village of Eamont Bridge in the English county of Cumbria, around one mile south east of Penrith [1]. It is 400 metres from Mayburgh Henge [1]. The henge is around 90 metres in diameter [1]. The enclosed area is about 50 metres across; the ditch has a maximum width of 16 metres; the berm 7 metres; and the bank 13 metres [1]. Around 1664 William Dugdale sketched the remains, showing the two opposing entrances, and also showing that there were two standing stones, one each side of the northwest entrance [1]. These stones had disappeared when William Stukeley saw the monument in 1725 [1]. Excavations were undertaken in 1937 by R. G. Collingwood and continued in 1939 by Gerhard Bersu [1]. The excavations showed that the ditch had been cleared out and reshaped and the entrance through it made narrower in modern times [1].
row.card: Around 1664, William Dugdale drew two standing stones by one entrance of this henge. By the time William Stukeley saw the Neolithic monument, both stones had disappeared.

row.description: Balankanche is an ancient Maya cave site lying at short distance from the archaeological Maya-Toltec city of Chichen Itza [1]. For more than two thousand years, it has been the focus of rituals dedicated to the Maya rain god, Chaac, and, in the Post-Classic period, also to his Toltec counterpart, Tlaloc [1]. The cave complex was visited by Edward Thompson and Alfred Tozzer in 1905 and has since 1932 been explored and studied by various Mexican and US scholars [1]. Small buildings and platforms surrounded the cave's entrance; inside, stairs, walls, altars and ritual displays of ceramics and small stone implements were discovered [1].
row.card: Rituals for the Maya rain god Chaac centred on this cave. Pottery finds point to ceremonies from 300 BC up to 1200, later also for his Toltec counterpart, Tlaloc.

row.description: High Peak is a hill which is partially eroded, resulting in a cliff face, on the English Channel coast to the southwest of Sidmouth, Devon, southern England [1]. Its highest point is about 157 metres above sea-level [1]. It features a partially eroded Iron Age hill fort, with pre-Roman and post Roman pottery found there [1]. On the edge of the cliff there are the remains of significant earthworks, which have been variously shown as having Iron Age, Roman and Dark Age occupation [1]. Geological study, and the lines of the earthworks, suggest that the site once extended several tens of metres into what is now eroded away [1]. General interpretation suggests that it was an Iron Age defensive site which saw re-use in the Dark Age period, perhaps as a coastal trading station [1].
row.card: Several tens of metres of this hill fort may now be eroded away. Earthworks line the cliff edge, and the fort was perhaps reused in the Dark Ages as a coastal trading station.

row.description: Oushiko Shrine is a Shinto shrine located on the slopes of Hōden Mountain in Takasago City, Hyogo Prefecture, Japan [1] [2]. The shrine enshrines a massive stone structure known as the "Stone Hōden" (石の宝殿), revered as the shrine's sacred object of worship [1] [3]. Oushiko Shrine is classified as one of Japan's "Three Mysteries" (日本三奇), together with Shiogama Shrine's salt cauldron in Miyagi Prefecture and Kirishima Higashi Shrine's Heavenly Reverse Halberd in Miyazaki Prefecture [1] [3].
row.card: The country's Three Mysteries include this shrine on a mountain slope. The others are a salt cauldron and a halberd at two other shrines; this one reveres a massive stone structure.

row.description: The Arch of Hadrian is an ancient Roman triumphal arch located in Santa Maria Capua Vetere (ancient Capua, now in the Province of Caserta, southern Italy) [1]. It was originally a triple arch, but today only three pylons and one of the lateral arches survive [1]. It spanned the Appian Way and constituted an ideal entrance to the city, perhaps corresponding to the line of the pomerium [1]. The arch was erected between the latter half of the 1st century and the former half of the 2nd century, but we are ignorant of its dedication [1]. The arch is constructed in brick and originally had an outer coating of white limestone, now lost [1]. The remains extend to a height of 10 metres and a width of 18.5 metres [1].
row.card: A coat of white limestone, now lost, once covered this brick arch. Once a triple arch, the Roman triumphal arch spanned the Appian Way as a symbolic entrance to the city.

row.description: Roman Ridge is a bridleway that was part of the Roman road of Ermine Street, between Scawsby and Redhouse to the north of Doncaster [1]. This footpath departs from the A638 road at The Sun junction with the A635 (or Barnsley Road) [1]. Its course runs at an angle bisecting the angle made between the two modern roads [1]. It runs to the west of the A638, roughly parallel to it, through the area of Sunnyfields and on to cross Green Lane, Scawsby on the eastern edge of Little Canada [1]. From there it runs along the western edge of the villages of Highfields and Woodlands until it reaches the Red House junction of the Great North Road [1]. From there, the Roman Ridge joins the A1 as far as Barnsdale [1].
row.card: Ermine Street, a Roman road, once ran along this bridleway. Today the path cuts in half the angle between two modern roads, then skirts two villages to meet the Great North Road.

row.description: Castro, in the province of Lecce, Apulia, is the ancient Castrum Minervae mentioned by Virgil in the Aeneid as the first Italian landfall of Aeneas after fleeing Troy [1] [2] [3]. The settlement dates to the Iron Age (8th century BC) and was occupied by Messapians and Greeks [4] [5]. University of Salento excavations directed by Francesco D'Andria from 2000 onward uncovered a sanctuary dedicated to Athena Iliaca, including a 12-cm bronze statue of the goddess wearing a Phrygian helmet (4th century BC), decorative stone slabs with winged Victories, and votive weapons [4] [6] [7]. Hellenistic-era Messapian walls from the 4th century BC were also discovered [4] [8]. The sanctuary functioned until the 3rd century BC, when it was violently destroyed, possibly during Hannibal's campaigns in 214 BC [4] [9]. Finds are displayed at the Antonio Lazzari Archaeological Museum in Castro Castle [2] [10].
row.card: Virgil has Aeneas, fleeing Troy, first land in this country at this old town. Digs uncovered a sanctuary of Athena, with a 12-cm bronze statue of her in a Phrygian helmet.

row.description: Hound Tor is a tor on Dartmoor, Devon, England and is a good example of a heavily weathered granite outcrop [1]. The site is administered by Dartmoor National Park Authority for English Heritage as it includes the ruins of a medieval village, alongside prehistoric works of stone construction nearby [1]. To the southeast of the tor, on a northeast-facing slope are the remains of Hundatorra, a deserted medieval village [1]. This was built on land farmed originally in the Bronze Age and which may have been used for grazing in the Roman period [1]. The village was excavated between 1961 and 1975 [1]. It has four Dartmoor longhouses, many with a central drainage channel, and several smaller houses and barns [1]. These buildings date from the 13th century [1].
row.card: A deserted medieval village lies beside a heavily weathered granite outcrop. The village rose on land originally farmed in the Bronze Age, and maybe grazed in the Roman period.

row.description: The burial ground of Cherneliv-Ruskyi is a burial site of the Chernyakhov culture, an archaeological monument of local importance [1]. It is located in the Mohylky tract of the village of Cherneliv-Ruskyi in the Baikivtsi Hromada of the Ternopil Raion of the Ternopil Oblast [1]. The site was investigated between 1973 and 2000 by Ukrainian archaeologist Ihor Gereta [1]. During the excavations, 315 burials were discovered, including 288 Chernyakhov, 24 Kievan Rus', two Pomeranian, and one unidentified burial, probably dating from the Bronze Age [1].
row.card: One grave here, not identified, probably dates from the Bronze Age. Digs by Ihor Gereta found 315 burials in all, among them 24 from Kievan Rus' and two Pomeranian ones.

row.description: The oldest known monumental sculpture in Egypt, carved from a single mass of limestone on the Giza Plateau [1]. Measuring approximately 73 metres long and 20 metres high, it depicts a reclining lion with a human head wearing a royal headdress [1] [2] [3]. The Sphinx sits adjacent to the causeway connecting Khafre's valley temple to his mortuary temple, though some scholars propose his brother Redjedef or father Khufu as the commissioner [1] [2] [4]. Researchers estimate 100 workers spent three years carving it using stone hammers and copper chisels [5].
row.card: About 73 metres long, a reclining lion with a human head wears a royal headdress. By one estimate, 100 workers spent three years carving the figure with stone hammers and copper chisels.

row.description: Gemellae was a Roman fort and associated camp on the fringe of the Sahara Desert in what is today part of Algeria [1]. It is now an archaeological site, 25 km south and 19 km west of Biskra, and 5 km southwest of the present-day village of M'Lili with which it probably shares an original Berber name [1]. It was connected by military Roman road to Castellum Dimmidi and Capsa [1]. The earliest epigraph retrieved from the site is an inscription for a statue of Emperor Hadrian, in about the year 126 AD, by a cohors equitata originating from Chalcis in Syria [1]. A second very large dedication to Hadrian, which faced the central courtyard, dates from 132 AD [1]. The great fort of Gemellae is rectangular with sides oriented to the cardinal directions, constructed in a manner common to most Roman castra [1]. It measures 150 metres north to south and 190 m east to west [1]. For the most part, the masonry wall was about 3 metres thick, using stone from a quarry 14 kilometres distant [1].
row.card: The earliest inscription found here was for a statue of Emperor Hadrian. Soldiers from Chalcis in Syria made that dedication in about 126 AD, at a Roman fort on the fringe of the Sahara.

row.description: The Rutland Roman villa is a Romano-British villa site near Ketton in Rutland, England [1]. The villa includes the first example of a Roman mosaic in Britain which depicts scenes from the Trojan War [1]. A geophysical survey of the site in 2021 showed evidence of a large villa complex including indications of a formal garden, a bath house, perhaps a chapel and two mausolea [1]. The site was first identified from cropmarks visible on Google Earth in June 2018 [1]. The mosaic measures 11 metres by nearly 7 metres [1].
row.card: The first Roman mosaic in Britain with scenes from the Trojan War lies at this villa. Photos of the villa's cropmarks were taken in June 2018 and later made widely available on Google Earth.

row.description: The Temple of Aphaia is an Ancient Greek temple located within a sanctuary complex dedicated to the goddess Aphaia on the island of Aegina, which lies in the Saronic Gulf [1]. Formerly known as the Temple of Jupiter Panhellenius, the Doric temple is now recognized as having been dedicated to the mother-goddess Aphaia [1]. Aphaia was a Greek goddess who was worshipped exclusively at this sanctuary [1]. The extant temple of c. 500 BC was built over the remains of an earlier temple of c. 570 BC, which was destroyed by fire c. 510 BC [1]. The last temple is of an unusual plan and is also significant for its pedimental sculptures, which are thought to illustrate the change from Archaic to Early Classical technique [1]. These sculptures are on display in the Glyptothek of Munich [1]. The temple was a hexastyle peripteral Doric order structure on a 6 by 12 column plan resting on a 15.5 by 30.5 m platform; it had a distyle in antis cella with an opisthodomos and a pronaos [1].
row.card: Fire destroyed an earlier temple of this island sanctuary. Around 500 BC a new temple rose over the remains, and the new temple's pediment sculptures are now on display in Munich.

row.description: La Pintada is an archaeological site located some 60 kilometers south of the city of Hermosillo, Sonora, Mexico, within the "La Pintada" canyon, part of the "Sierra Libre" [1]. La Pintada comprises two different archaeological components; within the Canyon are cave paintings and rock engravings, while outside, on the alluvial plain of the Canyon are vestiges of various seasonal camping grounds in an extensive area, characterized by a concentration of archaeological material: ceramic, stone tools [1]. Most of the archaeological materials found in these grounds, are within the archaeological tradition known as Central Coast, and are particularly similar to those found by Edward Mosler and Thomas Bowen at sites in the region of Tastiota and Punta San Antonio in the southern part of the Central Coast area [1]. So far, La Pintada is the site associated with that archaeological tradition farther away from the coastline [1].
row.card: No site of the Central Coast tradition known so far lies farther from the coastline. Paintings and engravings mark the canyon, and camps on the plain outside left pottery and stone tools.

row.description: The Ridgeway is a ridgeway or ancient trackway described as Britain's oldest road [1]. The section clearly identified as an ancient trackway extends from Wiltshire along the chalk ridge of the Berkshire Downs to the River Thames at the Goring Gap, part of the Icknield Way which ran, not always on the ridge, from Salisbury Plain to East Anglia [1]. For at least 5,000 years travellers have used the Ridgeway [1]. The Ridgeway provided a reliable trading route to the Dorset coast and to the Wash in Norfolk [1]. The high dry ground made travel easy and provided a measure of protection by giving traders a commanding view, warning against potential attacks [1]. During the Iron Age, inhabitants took advantage of the high ground by building hillforts along the Ridgeway to help defend the trading route [1].
row.card: Described as Britain's oldest road, this trackway has a stretch on a chalk ridge. Iron Age people built hillforts along the track, and that stretch runs to the Thames at the Goring Gap.

row.description: Furby is a locality in Badelunda parish, Vasteraas Municipality, Sweden, situated near Anundshog -- Sweden's largest burial mound (9 m high, 64 m diameter), built between the 5th and 11th centuries AD [1] [2] [3]. The area served as a gathering place for legal assemblies (Things) and lay at the crossroads of major trade routes linking Lake Malar communities with northern regions [3].
row.card: Legal assemblies gathered at this crossroads of major trade routes. The routes linked Lake Malar communities with the north, and the country's largest burial mound rises nearby.

row.description: The Trier Amphitheater is a Roman amphitheater in Trier, Germany [1]. The structure which was dug into the side of a hill was erected around the 2nd century A.D during the rule of Antoninus Pius [1]. Measuring 120 by 145 meters, the amphitheatre could accommodate approximately 20,000 spectators and is the 10th largest Roman amphitheatre still intact [1]. It was built into what was at the time the city's wall, to the east of the modern and Roman city centre [1]. When Constantius Chlorus moved to Trier, Germany around 293 during the Tetrarchy he renovated the amphitheater [1]. On the eastern bank of the amphitheatre, a small burial ground was discovered in 1996, containing the graves of 46 people [1].
row.card: When Constantius Chlorus moved to the city, he renovated this Roman arena. The arena, dug into a hillside and built into what was then the city's wall, could hold about 20,000 spectators.

row.description: Thebes, known to the ancient Egyptians as Waset, was an ancient Egyptian city located along the Nile about 800 kilometers south of the Mediterranean [1]. Its ruins lie within the modern Egyptian city of Luxor [1]. Thebes was the main city of the fourth Upper Egyptian nome and was the capital of Egypt for long periods during the Middle Kingdom and New Kingdom eras [1]. The site of Thebes includes areas on both the eastern bank of the Nile, where the temples of Karnak and Luxor stand and where the city was situated; and the western bank, where a necropolis of large private and royal cemeteries and funerary complexes can be found [1]. Thebes was inhabited from around 3200 BC [1]. Ahmose I founded a new age for a unified Egypt with Thebes as its capital [1]. Thebes was home to several major monuments of ancient Egypt including the temples of Luxor and Karnak, along with the Valley of the Kings and the Valley of the Queens [1].
row.card: Ahmose founded a new age for a unified land, ruled from this city. On the Nile's east bank stand the temples of Karnak and Luxor; royal cemeteries spread over the west bank.

row.description: Dalton Parlours Roman villa is a Roman villa and scheduled monument near Collingham, West Yorkshire [1]. The site was discovered in 1854 on land owned by the Lady Elizabeth Hastings Charities and excavated by F Carroll in 1855 [1]. These initial excavations located two buildings with hypocausts and the Medusa mosaic [1]. A rescue excavation in 1977 excavated 3.5 acres of the site [1]. The modern excavations discovered an Iron Age site beneath the Roman villa [1]. The villa was constructed in the 3rd-century AD, though some evidence suggests 2nd-century activity at the site as well [1]. Coins on the site date from AD 270–355 [1].
row.card: A mosaic of Medusa turned up in the early digs at this Roman villa. Those digs also found two buildings with underfloor heating, and modern digs found an Iron Age site beneath the villa.

row.description: Hatun Uchku is a cave with archaeological and paleontological remains in Peru [1]. It was declared a National Cultural Heritage by Resolución Directoral No. 441/INC on May 23, 2002 [1]. Hatun Uchku is situated in the Huánuco Region, Ambo Province, Ambo District, about 500 m south of the main square of Ambo, at a height of 2,206 metres [1].
row.card: Fossils and traces of people turn up in this cave. In 2002 the cave was declared National Cultural Heritage, and the cave lies about 500 m south of a town's main square.

row.description: The Taghlar cave is an archaeological site that was inhabited by prehistoric humans of the Mousterian culture during the Paleolithic [1]. The cave is located in Azerbaijan, in the disputed region of Nagorno-Karabakh, in the southern part of Boyuk Taghlar village, on the left banks of the Guruchay River [1]. Ancient people lived here 64-24 thousand years ago [1]. The cave was discovered during the Paleolithic archaeological expedition of Academy of Science of Azerbaijan under the leadership of M.Huseynov in 1960 [1]. Beginning in 1963, archaeological excavations were carried out in the cave and more than 7,000 stone tools and over 2,000 faunal fossilized bones were discovered and six cultural sediment layers were identified at the site [1]. Indices of the Mousterian culture were found in between the 2nd and 6th layer [1]. The remains of large mammals such as horse, noble deer, bull were found in the 5th layer [1].
row.card: More than 7,000 stone tools have been dug from this riverside cave. Stone Age people lived in the cave, and one of its six layers held remains of mammals such as horse, noble deer and bull.

row.description: Huerfano Butte (English: "Orphan Butte") is a small rocky butte located on the western flank of the Santa Rita Mountains in southeastern Pima County, Arizona [1]. Huerfano Butte and the surrounding area were utilized by the Hohokam as early as circa 1100 CE [1]. Shallow bedrock forces ground water to surface in a small pool located in a wash on the south side of the butte [1]. Exposed outcrops of granite on either side of the wash have about fifty bedrock mortars, at least two small bedrock metates, and numerous smaller cupules [1]. Along the same wash is a vertical stone surface with approximately two dozen weathered pictographs painted in red hematite [1]. In 1965, Huerfano Butte gained public notoriety when a young girl discovered an extensive prehistoric jewelry cache while on a picnic with her family [1]. While exploring cracks and crevices on the butte, the young girl discovered a small pottery jar filled with about 1,500 turquoise and glycimeris shell beads and pendants [1].
row.card: A young girl on a picnic found prehistoric jewelry on this small rocky hill. Granite outcrops on either side of a wash hold about fifty bedrock mortars and many smaller hollows.

row.description: The Puente de Alcántara is a Roman arch bridge in Toledo spanning the River Tagus [1]. The word Alcántara comes from Arabic القنطرة, which means "arch" [1]. Located at the foot of the Castillo de San Servando, it was built by the Romans after they founded the city [1]. During the reign of Alfonso X of Castile it suffered serious damage due to flooding and was rebuilt [1]. The western tower belongs to this period, later decorated under the reign of the Catholic Monarchs, whose arms decorate its walls [1]. The eastern tower was replaced by a Baroque triumphal arch in 1721, because of its ruinous state [1]. It was declared a national cultural monument in 1921 [1].
row.card: A Baroque triumphal arch replaced the eastern tower of this Roman bridge in 1721. The western tower dates from a rebuild after a flood and bears the arms of the Catholic Monarchs.

row.description: Dun Dornaigil is an Iron Age broch in Sutherland in the Scottish Highlands [1]. It is in Strathmore on the eastern bank of the Strathmore River [1]. The broch has an external diameter of about 14.5 metres [1]. The walls of Dun Dornaigil generally survive from 2 to 3 metres around the circumference of the broch, but above the doorway they rise to nearly 7 metres [1]. The entrance is on the northeast side but is filled with debris [1]. There is a massive triangular lintel over the entrance which measures 1.4 metres along the base, and 0.9 metres in height [1]. The interior of the broch is still filled with collapsed rubble from the upper levels and is therefore not accessible [1].
row.card: Walls nearly 7 metres high still rise above the doorway of this Iron Age broch. Rubble fallen from the upper levels chokes the inside, and a massive triangular lintel spans the door.

row.description: Acumincum was an ancient Roman settlement, located in the present day town of Stari Slankamen, Serbia [1]. In the 3rd century BC, the area was inhabited by Celtic Scordisci [1]. The name also appears as Acimincum and in the Peutingerian Table, the name is written Acunum [1]. Jupiter Dolichenus sculptures have been found in the town [1].
row.card: Sculptures of Jupiter Dolichenus have been found in this ancient Roman settlement. In the 3rd century BC, the area was inhabited by a people called the Scordisci.

row.description: Bignor Roman Villa is a large Roman courtyard villa which has been excavated and put on public display on the Bignor estate in the English county of West Sussex [1]. It is well known for its high quality mosaic floors, which are some of the most complete and intricate in the country [1]. The existence of a Romano-British farmstead on the site by the end of the 1st century is indicated by finds, but the earliest structural remains are of a simple timber farm structure dating to around 190 AD [1]. A four-roomed stone building was built in the middle of the 3rd century AD, and this was extended between c.240 and 290 AD by the addition of a few new rooms, a hypocaust, and a portico that faced east towards Stane Street [1]. This building became the western wing when north and south wings were added at the turn of the fourth century [1]. In its final form, the villa consisted of some sixty-five rooms surrounding a courtyard [1]. The latest phase of building involved additions to the north wing between c.300 and 350 AD, and it is here that most of the fine mosaics are located [1].
row.card: Some sixty-five rooms once ringed the courtyard of this large Roman villa. Its north wing holds most of the fine mosaics, floors among the most complete and intricate in the country.

row.description: The Cerro Pátapo ruins or Northern Wari ruins are the remains of a pre-Columbian city near the site of present-day Chiclayo, Peru [1]. The ruins are primarily of the Wari (Huari) culture [1]. The discovery was announced on 16 December 2008 by the lead archeologist, Cesar Soriano [1]. The city was part of the Wari Empire, which ruled parts of the Andes Mountains, mostly in south-central Peru [1]. The site is remarkably well preserved due to the dry desert climate [1]. The site includes evidence of human sacrifice, with special spots set aside and a pile of bones at the bottom of a cliff [1]. Well-preserved remains have been found of one young woman [1].
row.card: A pile of bones lies at the bottom of a cliff in this ruined city. Special spots were set aside for human sacrifice, and the remains of one young woman were found well preserved.

row.description: Glevum was originally a Roman fort in Roman Britain that became a "colonia" of retired legionaries in AD 97 [1]. Today, it is known as Gloucester, in the English county of Gloucestershire [1]. In AD 97, the city was designated a colonia by the Emperor Nerva [1]. The legionaries were given farmland in the surrounding district, and could be called upon as a Roman auxiliary armed force [1]. The city was built within the legionary fortress and used the same rectilinear street plan and ramparts [1]. A large and impressive administrative basilica and forum market-place were built in the town, as well as many fine homes with mosaic floors [1]. Excavations at Gloucester's New Market Hall in the 1960s showed that Romano-British occupation of the town may have continued in some form into the sub-Roman period, even if the town's population may have been greatly reduced [1].
row.card: Retired Roman soldiers were given farmland around this town. The town rose inside the old fort, kept the fort's street plan and ramparts, and gained fine homes with mosaic floors.

row.description: The Mount William stone axe quarry (traditionally known as Wil-im-ee moor-ing) is an Aboriginal Australian archaeological site in Central Victoria [1]. Known as Wil-im-ee moor-ring, meaning "axe place" in the Woiwurrung language, the greenstone quarry was an important source of raw material for the manufacture of greenstone ground-edge axes [1]. The Mount William Aboriginal stone axe quarry comprises the remains of hundreds of mining pits and the mounds of waste rock where Aboriginal people obtained greenstone, and manufactured stone blanks for axe heads [1]. The stone was quarried from the source outcrops, and roughly flaked into blanks, then taken away for finer flaking and grinding the edge [1]. There are 268 mining pits, 18 of which are several metres deep, surrounded by at least 34 discrete flaking floors, with mounds of debris up to 20 metres in diameter and some featuring a central outcropping rock used as an anvil [1]. Mount William had long been recognised as a special Aboriginal place when the first attempt was made to provide some formal protection in 1910 [1].
row.card: Aboriginal people mined greenstone from 268 pits at this site. Waste rock still lies in mounds up to 20 metres across, some with a central rock used as an anvil.

row.description: The Temple of Athena Alea was a sanctuary at Tegea in Ancient Greece, dedicated to Athena under the epithet Athena Alea; a syncretization between the Olympian goddess Athena and the local deity Alea [1]. It was a significant Greek temple [1]. The first temple at the site likely dates to the early Archaic period of Greek history; the memory of this temple survived, and is included in the account of Pausanias [1]. The cult statue of the Athena Alea was made by Endoeus in ivory [1].
row.card: An ivory cult statue by Endoeus once stood in this sanctuary. Tests on slag found in front of its Geometric temple confirmed that metal was worked there at that time.

row.description: Hohlenstein-Stadel is a cave located in the Hohlenstein cliff (not to be confused with the Hohle Fels) at the southern rim of the Lonetal in the Swabian Jura in Germany [1]. The most significant finding was a small ivory statue called the Löwenmensch, which is one of the oldest pieces of figurative art ever found [1]. The first excavations at Hohlenstein were made in 1861 by Oskar Fraas, geologist and paleontologist [1]. On 27 August 1937, excavators discovered the right femur diaphysis, measuring around 25 cm in length, of an archaic hominin in the cave [1]. The femur came from a layer associated with Middle Paleolithic Mousterian artefacts [1]. In 2017, researchers successfully sequenced the full mtDNA genome from the femur [1]. The results confirmed that the femur belonged to a Neanderthal [1].
row.card: A small ivory statue called the Löwenmensch came from this cave. The statue is among the oldest pieces of figurative art ever found, and a thigh bone from the cave belonged to a Neanderthal.

row.description: The San Estevan archaeological site is located in northern Belize 1 km from the modern community of San Estevan [1]. The site is a Maya civilization site occupied during the Formative (800 BC – AD 300) and Classic (AD 300 – 900) eras of Mesoamerican chronology [1]. San Estevan is located on the New River halfway between the sites of Cerros and Lamanai [1]. Beginning in the Late Formative period, San Estevan was a regional political center [1]. William Bullard mapped the civic-ceremonial center of the site in the 1960s where he carried out excavations and restored two Early Classic structures (I and II) [1]. In 1989 and 1990, Laura Levi mapped outlying house groups at San Estevan in detail and excavated several domestic structures [1]. Mound XV, at 15 m, is the highest structure remaining at the site and dates to the Late Formative period [1].
row.card: A mound 15 metres high is the highest structure left at this Maya site. The mound dates to the Late Formative, when the site became a regional political center on the New River.
